newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese president says fight poverty with fervour.
newsitem.headline: Chinese president says fight poverty with fervour.

text.p: China's Communist Party chief and state president Jiang Zemin has found a new weapon to fight poverty -- resurrect communist revolutionary fervour.
Jiang visited villagers in some of China's poorest regions and told them poverty relief was a political problem, the People's Daily, mouthpiece of the Communist Party, said on Monday.

"Solving the problem of adequate food and clothing for poor people in farming villages is not only an economic problem, it is also a political problem," Jiang said last week during an inspection tour of a new showcase railway that will eventually link Beijing to Hong Kong's Kowloon district.

Jiang exhorted villagers and officials to resurrect the "glorious tradition" of the revolution that swept the communists into power in 1949. Revolutionary fervour died after almost two decades of economic reforms which set people free to get rich.
"(I) hope the broad masses of cadres and people will continue to uphold the zeal and spirit of the revolutionary war era...to accelerate the pace of their escape from poverty," Jiang said.
China estimates it has about 65 million people struggling to get by with incomes under the official absolute poverty line of 530 yuan ($64) a year.
Beijing fears that uneven economic growth between booming coastal provinces and the backward interior could spark social unrest and undermine the Communist Party's grip on power.
Jiang, eager to shore up his political position, has repeatedly borrowed wording and imagery from the ideologically charged days of Chairman Mao Zedong when revolutionary fervour was at its zenith.

Jiang wrapped up his rail journey with a visit to the southern boomtown of Shenzhen across the border from the British colony of Hong Kong, which reverts to Chinese rule on July 1, 1997, the newspaper said.
He said the new Beijing-Kowloon railway would help guarantee the prosperity of post-1997 Hong Kong by giving the capitalist territory easier access to China's interior.
